content: The systematic review did not report on postnatal care outcomes, including breastfeeding status or adverse effects. One trial involving 70 women compared oral serrapeptase (Danzen), an anti-inflammatory proteolytic enzyme derived from Serratia E15 (isolated from silkworm intestines), with a placebo. The trial authors provided cumulative percentages in the results, which were later corrected by the review authors. Breastfeeding was encouraged during the study, but only four women in the treatment group and eight in the placebo group breastfed their babies during the trial period. For the comparison of subcutaneous oxytocin with placebo, the evidence was of very low certainty. The desirable and undesirable effects, as well as the balance of effects, were uncertain. The required resources were considered to have moderate costs, but no studies were included to evaluate cost-effectiveness. Equity and feasibility varied, and acceptability was deemed probably low. The WHO recommendations for maternal and newborn care emphasize a positive postnatal experience. However, it remains uncertain whether oral serrapeptase has any effect on breast pain or swelling compared to placebo, as the evidence is of very low certainty. Similarly, its impact on adverse effects is also uncertain due to the low certainty of the narrative evidence. Short-term maternal morbidity, health service use, maternal functioning/well-being, and experiences of postnatal care were not reported in the systematic review. Outcomes related to newborns or infants, including breastfeeding status and adverse effects, were also not reported. The included trials reported no adverse effects in either the protease, serrapeptase, or placebo groups. Serrapeptase and bromelain are marketed as dietary or nutritional supplements and are widely available without a prescription. However, a systematic review concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support the use of serrapeptase as an analgesic or health supplement. No economic evaluations of pharmacological interventions for treating breast engorgement were identified. Additionally, no direct evidence was found regarding the impact of pharmacological interventions on health equity for treating breast engorgement following childbirth. Proteolytic enzymes may be prohibitively expensive for some women, potentially decreasing equity. Their availability likely varies by region, but they may have no effect on or even increase equity if provided by health facilities. Mastitis is an inflammatory condition of the breast characterized by pain, redness, and swelling, which may or may not be accompanied by infection. Approximately one in four breastfeeding women experience mastitis within the first 26 weeks postpartum. Non-infective mastitis may result from milk stasis, blocked ducts, engorgement, or tissue damage often associated with poor infant positioning and attachment or incomplete breast emptying. Infective mastitis may result from cracked or traumatized nipples and can lead to abscess formation. Preventing mastitis typically involves effective milk removal, ensuring good infant positioning and attachment, massaging the breast during feeding, and supportive measures such as rest, adequate fluid intake, warm compresses, and oral analgesia. Postpartum constipation, defined as infrequent, hard, dry, or bulky stools that are difficult or painful to pass, affects 15–62% of women. Disrupted eating during active labor and the immediate postpartum period, as well as cultural practices, dietary restrictions, and emotional concerns, may negatively affect bowel movements. Preventive measures include dietary and lifestyle modifications and advice on positioning during bowel movements. The WHO guidelines on preventing maternal infections relevant to routine postnatal care include recommendations for preventing mastitis. Women should be counseled and supported to practice responsive breastfeeding, ensure good positioning and attachment of the baby to the breast, hand express breast milk, and use warm or cold compresses based on their preferences. Responsive breastfeeding involves the mother responding to her baby’s cues as well as her own desire to breastfeed. This approach recognizes the reciprocal mother-baby relationship and the benefits of breastfeeding beyond hunger alleviation. All women should be informed about common breast conditions associated with lactation, such as sore or cracked nipples, engorgement, and mastitis, and encouraged to report any signs or symptoms to their care providers. Providers should support women in continuing breastfeeding with breast engorgement if they wish to, as per the 2017 WHO guidelines on breastfeeding in maternity and newborn care facilities. Breastfeeding counseling should be provided to all women in accordance with the 2018 WHO guidelines on improving breastfeeding practices. Evidence from a Cochrane systematic review on interventions for preventing mastitis after childbirth included 10 trials with 3034 women. Both pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions were evaluated separately. Six trials (2215 women) evaluated non-pharmacological interventions, including probiotics, hydrothermally processed cereals, in-hospital specialist breastfeeding education, and breast acupoint massage. Probiotics were given daily in capsule form containing Lactobacillus fermentum in one trial. However, results from the largest trial (639 women) were unavailable due to contractual restrictions. It is uncertain whether probiotics reduce nipple damage or breast pain within six months postpartum, as the evidence is of very low certainty. Maternal functioning, well-being, adverse effects, health service use, and postnatal care experiences were not reported in the included trials. Probiotics may be prohibitively expensive for some women, potentially decreasing equity. Cold storage requirements for some probiotics may limit their availability in under-resourced settings. It is unlikely that probiotics will be supplied by health services, but if they are, they may have no effect on or even increase equity. Despite the recognized health, emotional, psychosocial, and societal benefits of breastfeeding, global breastfeeding rates remain suboptimal, particularly among low-income women. Preventing breast problems that may affect breastfeeding continuation would not only improve health outcomes for mothers and infants but also reduce the economic burden on this group within the community. Women often feel unprepared for the challenges associated with breastfeeding and would welcome more information and support to enable informed decision-making regarding breastfeeding techniques and treatments for painful or uncomfortable breasts. Techniques or treatments that provide relief from breast engorgement are likely to enhance the mother-infant relationship, improve body image, and increase psychosocial well-being. In some contexts, women may prefer traditional practices, including diet, medicinal plants, massage, and spiritual healing, to enhance breastfeeding and address associated problems. Probiotics in sachets, tablets, or capsules are anticipated to be acceptable to most women. No economic evaluations of non-pharmacological interventions for preventing mastitis following childbirth were identified.
